source_text:
Ἃ δὲ ἁπάντων ἐστὶ κορυφαιότατα, καὶ ὧν μάλιστα ἕνεκα πᾶν τὸ φιλόσοφον διαπονεῖται γένος, ὥσπερ ἐκ φυτείας ποικίλης τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων μαθημάτων καὶ φιλοσοφίας μακρᾶς καρποὺς ἀγαθοὺς ἐκδεχόμενον, τὰς θείας ἀρετὰς τὰς περὶ ἦθος, ἐξ ὧν ἡ ἀτάραχος καὶ εὐσταθὴς τῶν ὁρμῶν τῆς ψυχῆς κατάστασις γίνεται· καὶ ἀλύπους μὲν καὶ ἀπαθεῖς ἁπάντων κακῶν, εὐτάκτους δὲ καὶ εὐσταθεῖς καὶ θεοειδεῖς ἤμελλεν ἡμᾶς ὄντως καὶ μακαρίους καταστήσεσθαι. καὶ ταῦτα δὲ ἐξεπονεῖτο λόγοις τε ἰδίοις πραΰνουσι καὶ σοφοῖς, οὐχ ἥκιστα καὶ ἀναγκαιοτάτοις, περὶ τῶν ἠθῶν καὶ τῶν τρόπων ἡμῶν. καὶ οὐ λόγοις μόνον, ἀλλ' ἤδη καὶ ἔργοις τρόπον τινὰ διεκυβερνᾶτο παρ' ἡμῶν τὰς ὁρμάς, αὐτῇ τῇ τῶν ὁρμῶν καὶ παθῶν τῶν τῆς ψυχῆς θεωρίᾳ καὶ κατανοήσει· ἐξ ἧς μάλιστα κατεγνωσμένης κατορθοῦσθαι ἐξ ἀναρμοστίας πέφυκεν ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχή, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ κεκριμένον καὶ εὔτακτον ἐκ συγκεχυμένης μετατίθεσθαι· ἵν' ὥσπερ ἐν κατόπτρῳ ἑαυτὴν θεωρήσασα, αὐτὰς τὰς ἀρχὰς καὶ ῥίζας τῶν κακῶν, τὸ ἄλογον αὐτῆς πᾶν, ἐξ οὗ τὰ ἄτοπα ἡμῖν ἐπανίσταται πάθη· καὶ πάλιν ὅσον ἄριστον αὐτῆς μέρος λογικόν, ὑφ' οὗ κρατοῦντος μένει γε ὑφ' ἑαυτῆς ἀβλαβὴς καὶ ἀπαθής· εἶτα ταῦτα ἐν αὐτῇ κατανοήσασα ἀκριβῶς, πάντα μὲν τὰ ἐκ τοῦ χείρονος ἐκφυόμενα, ἐκχέοντα ἡμᾶς ὑπὸ ἀκολασίας, ἢ συστέλλοντα καὶ συμπνίγοντα ὑπὸ ταπεινότητος, οἷον ἡδονὰς καὶ ἐπιθυμίας, ἢ λύπας καὶ φόβους, καὶ ὅσος τοῖς γένεσι τοῖσδε ἕπεται στοῖχος κακῶν, ταῦτα μὲν ἐκβάλλοι καὶ ἐκποδὼν ποιοῖτο, ἔτι ἀρχομένοις καὶ ἄρτι φυομένοις ἐπανισταμένη, καὶ οὐκ ἐῶσα οὐδὲ μικρὸν αὔξειν, ἀλλ' ἀπολλύουσα καὶ ἐξαφανίζουσα· ὅσα δὲ ἐκ τοῦ κρείττονος ἀνατέλλει ἡμῖν ἀγαθὰ ὄντα, ταῦτα ἐκτρέφοι τε καὶ διασώζοι, καὶ ἀρχόμενα τιθηνοῦσα καὶ συμφυλάττουσα ἄχρι τελειότητος. οὕτω γὰρ ἄν ποτε παραγενέσθαι ψυχῇ τὰς θείας ἀρετάς· φρόνησίν τε τὴν αὐτὰ ταῦτα τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ κινήματα κρίνειν πρῶτον δυναμένην, ἐξ αὐτῶν καὶ τῆς περὶ τὰ ἔξω ἡμῶν, εἴ τινά ἐστιν, ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν ἐπιστήμης γενομένης· καὶ σωφροσύνην, τὴν ταῦτα ἐν ἀρχαῖς ὀρθῶς αἱρουμένην δύναμιν· καὶ δικαιοσύνην, ἣ τὰ ἄξια ἑκάστοις ἀπονέμει· καὶ τὴν πάντων τούτων σωτηρίαν, ἀνδρείαν.

Οὐ λόγοις τοίνυν ἀπαγγελλομένοις συνείθιζεν, ὡς δὴ εἴη ἐπιστήμη ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν, ἢ ποιητέων καὶ οὐ ποιητέων, ἡ φρόνησις· τοῦτο δὴ τὸ κενὸν καὶ ἀνωφελὲς μάθημα, εἰ ὁ λόγος εἴη τῶν ἔργων δίχα, καὶ φρόνησις οὐχὶ ποιοῦσα τὰ ποιητά, καὶ ἀποτρέπουσα τῶν οὐ ποιητῶν, γινώσκειν δὲ ταῦτα παρεχομένη τοῖς ἔχουσιν αὐτήν, οἵους πολλοὺς ὁρῶμεν. ἡ δὲ σωφροσύνη πάλιν, ὅτι δὴ εἴη τις ἐπιστήμη αἱρετῶν καὶ οὐχ αἱρετῶν, οὐ πάνυ τι διδασκόντων αὐτὴν τῶν ἄλλων φιλοσόφων, καὶ μάλιστά γε τῶν νεωτέρων, ὄντων μὲν εὐτόνων καὶ ἐρρωμένων τοῖς λόγοις (οἵους ἐγὼ πολλάκις ἐθαύμασα, ὅταν τὴν αὐτὴν ἀρετὴν Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς τὰ πρῶτα Θεῷ ἴσον εἶναι τὸν σοφὸν ἄνθρωπον ἀποδείξωσιν), οὔτε δὲ τὴν φρόνησιν, ὡς καὶ ποιεῖ τις τὰ φρονήσεως, οὔτε τὴν σωφροσύνην, ὡς καὶ αἱρεῖτό τις ταῦθ' ἅπερ ἔμαθε, παραδοῦναι δυναμένων. ὁμοίως δὲ κἀπὶ τῆς δικαιοσύνης, καὶ ἔτι τῆς ἀνδρείας. οὐχ οὕτως οὗτος τὰ περὶ ἀρετῶν ἡμῖν διεξῄει λόγοις, ἐπὶ δὲ τὰ ἔργα μᾶλλον παρεκάλει· καὶ παρεκάλει πλέον τοῖς ἔργοις, ἢ οἷς ἔλεγεν.
thought_title: Ethics: the soul sees itself and the virtues take root
orientation: Origen turns to ethics, teaching the soul to know itself and urging the virtues more by his deeds than by his words.
pass_a_gloss: What things are topmost of all, and for whose sake most of all the whole philosophic race toils, receiving good fruits as from a varied planting of all the other learnings and of long philosophy: the divine virtues about character, from which comes the untroubled and steady settled state of the impulses of the soul; and [which] were going to establish us truly free of grief and impassible toward all evils, well-ordered, steady, godlike, and blessed. And these he labored at with his own words, soothing and wise, not least also most necessary, about our characters and ways. And not with words only, but already also with deeds in some way he steered our impulses, by the very contemplation and observation of the impulses and passions of the soul; from which, once thoroughly known, our soul is by nature set right out of disharmony and moved over from confused to discerned and ordered; so that, having beheld itself as in a mirror — the very beginnings and roots of evils, all its irrational part, from which the out-of-place passions rise up in us; and again whatever is its best part, the rational, under whose ruling it remains by itself unharmed and impassible — then, having observed these exactly in itself, all the things growing out from the worse, pouring us out by licentiousness or contracting and choking us by abjectness, such as pleasures and desires, or griefs and fears, and whatever row of evils follows these kinds — these it might cast out and put out of the way, rising against them while still beginning and just growing, not allowing them to grow even a little, but destroying and obliterating them; and whatever, being good, springs up in us from the better, these it might rear and preserve, nursing them from the beginning and guarding them together until perfection. For thus at length the divine virtues would come to the soul: prudence, able first to judge these very movements of the soul, knowledge of goods and evils about things outside us too, if any are such, having come from them; and self-control, the power rightly choosing these in their beginnings; and justice, which assigns what is worthy to each; and the preservation of all these, courage. || Not then by words announced did he accustom us, that prudence is knowledge of goods and evils, or of things to be done and not to be done; that empty and useless lesson, if the word were apart from deeds, and prudence not doing the things to be done and turning away from those not to be done, but providing to its holders to know these, such as we see many. And self-control again, that it is a knowledge of things to be chosen and not chosen, the other philosophers not really teaching it at all, and especially the newer ones, being vigorous and strong in arguments, but able to hand down neither prudence, so that one also does the things of prudence, nor self-control, so that one also chooses what he learned. Likewise with justice, and also courage. Not so did this man go through the matters of virtues with us by words, but rather called us on to deeds; and called us more by deeds than by what he said.

pass_b_english: Then came the highest things of all, the chief reason why the whole tribe of philosophers labors, gathering good fruit, as it were, from a varied planting of every other study and of a long course of philosophy: the divine virtues of character. From them the impulses of the soul come into a calm and steady state, and they were going to make us free from grief and untouched by any evil, well ordered, steady, godlike and truly blessed. These too he worked at with discourses of his own, calming and wise and, not least, most needful, about our characters and our ways of life. And not with words alone: already, in a way, he steered our impulses by deeds as well, through the very study and observation of the impulses and passions of the soul. For once this is thoroughly grasped, our soul is by nature set right out of discord and brought from confusion to discernment and order. The aim was that the soul should look at itself as in a mirror: at the very beginnings and roots of evil, the whole irrational part of itself, from which unnatural passions rise up in us; and again at its best part, the rational, under whose rule it suffers no harm from itself and stays free of passion. Then, having observed these things in itself with care, it was to cast out and clear away everything that springs from the worse part, which either pours us out in license or cramps and chokes us in abjectness: pleasures and desires, griefs and fears, and the whole train of evils that follows these kinds. It was to rise against them while they are still beginning and just sprouting, and not let them grow even a little, but destroy them and wipe them out. Whatever good things rise in us from the better part, it was to nurture and preserve, nursing them from their beginning and guarding them until they reach maturity. For in this way, he said, the divine virtues may at last come to the soul: prudence, which can first judge these very movements of the soul, once knowledge has come from them of the goods and evils outside us as well, if there are any; self-control, the power that rightly chooses these things at their beginnings; justice, which gives each what is due; and courage, the safeguard of them all.

So he did not train us with recited words, as though prudence were ‘knowledge of goods and evils, or of what should be done and what should not’. That is an empty and useless lesson if the word stands apart from deeds, and prudence does not do what should be done and turn away from what should not, but only lets those who have it know these things, as we see so many do. So too with self-control, as though it were ‘a knowledge of what is to be chosen and what is not’: the other philosophers hardly teach it at all, especially the more recent ones. Vigorous and forceful in argument they are (I have often marveled at them when they prove that God and men have the same virtue, and that on earth the wise man is equal to God in the highest things), but they cannot hand on prudence so that a person actually does what prudence requires, nor self-control so that a person actually chooses what he has learned. The same holds for justice, and for courage too. This man did not go through the virtues with us like that, in words; he urged us rather toward the deeds, and he urged us more by what he did than by what he said.
notes: Copy-text: Greek column of the 1622 Paris Opera omnia (printed pp. 64-66), as in the source row. The opening sentence is an anacoluthon: the relative clause (Ἃ … τὰς θείας ἀρετάς) is resumed by ταῦτα in the next sentence; Pass B makes it a statement (‘Then came the highest things of all…’). ἤμελλεν is singular with a neuter plural antecedent, so the virtues, not Origen, are the subject of ‘were going to make us’. ἐξ ἧς μάλιστα κατεγνωσμένης: the feminine participle is taken with θεωρία/κατανόησις (‘once this is thoroughly grasped’); it could also be heard as the soul ‘convicted’ by its own scrutiny. The ἵνα clause with optatives (ἐκβάλλοι, ἐκτρέφοι) is rendered ‘the aim was that… it was to…’. μένει γε ὑφ' ἑαυτῆς (print; Bengel ἐφ') rendered ‘suffers no harm from itself’ (unharmed by itself). ταπεινότης here means abjectness or low spirits, not the Christian virtue of humility. The parenthesis on the newer philosophers reports the Stoic doctrine that God and the wise man share one virtue (τὰ πρῶτα Θεῷ ἴσον, print = Vossius; A τῷ πρώτῳ). ποιεῖ and αἱρεῖτο follow the print (Bengel ποιοῖ, Koetschau αἱροῖτο); the sense is unchanged. The mirror image is philosophical here; no Scripture allusion is cited.
